prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

PARIS, France (CNN)  -- Opposition lawmakers Tuesday ridiculed President Nicolas Sarkozy for taking France back into NATO's military command after more than 40 years, but were unable to stop the move when it came to a vote. French troops on patrol with the Afghan army as part of the NATO mission in Afghanistan. The National Assembly voted in favor of Sarkozy's plan, 329-238. Socialist Laurent Fabius, a former prime minister, told Prime Minister Francois Fillon: "You tell us this would mean more independence and more influence. It would probably mean less independence and less influence." The move did not technically require parliamentary approval, but the president's party scheduled the debate to give opponents a chance to voice their opinions -- and to show a majority backed it. Asking the National Assembly to vote on the issue also showed how sensitive the matter is in France. France was a founding member of the NATO alliance in 1949 but it left the military structure in 1966 amid friction with the United States. "To cooperate is to lose your independence," French President Charles de Gaulle said at the time. For the next 43 years, even though France selectively participated in NATO military operations, de Gaulle's principle remained the governing cornerstone of French foreign policy. If Paris took orders from NATO military commanders, it was reasoned, the nation would no longer have complete control of its destiny. Sarkozy, however, believes the opposite -- that cooperation in NATO is a guarantee of French independence. Rejoining NATO's military command, he argued, will give France a seat at the table for decision-making. From its earliest years, the organization's trans-Atlantic ties were strained because U.S. analysts warned that if the European allies failed to increase their contributions to the alliance, they risked losing the support of the United States, according to NATO. Meanwhile, the European nations felt the United States was trying to dominate the organization, according to NATO. De Gaulle's 1966 decision meant no French forces could be under permanent allied command and that France would have no participation in defense planning. In 1995, France rejoined NATO's military committee, which advises NATO's political authorities on military policy and strategy and provides guidance on military matters to NATO's strategic commanders. While France was still not a part of the military command, it contributed troops and funding to NATO activities, including actions in Kosovo and Afghanistan. Half of all French troops outside the country are assigned to NATO military operations. Opponents of Sarkozy's move -- who include some members of his party -- believe de Gaulle, not Sarkozy, had it right. They started a last-minute petition drive to stop his march back into NATO. "With this decision, France will return as a subordinate country and will lose its ability to represent another image in the world," said Nicolas Dupont-Aignan, a member of the French National Assembly. The president's allies calculate Sarkozy's move will strengthen Europe's hand on defense issues. "There will be more European weight in the way decisions will be made," said Louis Giscard d'Estaing, a member of the National Assembly's U.S. Friendship Committee. "Therefore, the balance of power between the USA and Europe will be re-established within this French move." CNN's Sunaina Karkarey and Jim Bittermann contributed to this report .

However, they failed to block the policy in the National Assembly, which approved it by 329 votes to 238.

French forces were already serving alongside the Afghan army as part of NATO’s operation in Afghanistan.

Former Prime Minister Laurent Fabius, a Socialist, challenged Prime Minister Francois Fillon’s claim that the change would increase France’s autonomy and international influence. Fabius argued that it was more likely to reduce both.

Although parliamentary authorization was not legally necessary, Sarkozy’s party arranged the debate so critics could present their arguments and the government could demonstrate that a majority supported the decision. Holding a vote also underscored the political sensitivity of NATO membership in France.

France helped establish NATO in 1949 but withdrew from the alliance’s integrated military structure in 1966 after tensions with the United States. President Charles de Gaulle’s position at the time was that military cooperation meant surrendering national independence.

That principle remained central to French foreign policy for the following 43 years, even as the country chose to participate in certain NATO operations. The prevailing argument was that accepting instructions from NATO commanders would prevent France from retaining full control over its own future.

Sarkozy took the opposite view. He maintained that full cooperation within NATO would protect French independence by giving Paris a direct role in shaping the alliance’s decisions.

According to NATO, trans-Atlantic relations had been difficult since the organization’s early years. American analysts warned that European members could lose U.S. backing unless they contributed more to the alliance, while European governments suspected Washington of seeking to control NATO.

Under de Gaulle’s 1966 policy, French troops could not be placed permanently under allied authority, and France was excluded from NATO defense planning.

In 1995, France returned to NATO’s military committee. That body advises the alliance’s political leadership on military strategy and policy and gives military guidance to NATO’s strategic commanders.

Although France still remained outside the integrated command system, it continued supplying personnel and money for NATO missions, including operations in Kosovo and Afghanistan. Half of all French military personnel deployed abroad were serving in NATO operations.

Critics of Sarkozy’s decision—including some politicians from his own party—believed de Gaulle’s approach had been correct. In a final effort to prevent the return, they organized a petition campaign.

National Assembly member Nicolas Dupont-Aignan warned that the decision would place France in a subordinate position and weaken its ability to offer the world an alternative vision.

Sarkozy’s supporters, by contrast, argued that the policy would increase Europe’s influence over defense matters. Louis Giscard d’Estaing, a member of the National Assembly’s U.S. Friendship Committee, said Europe would carry greater weight in NATO decision-making and that France’s return would help restore the balance of power between Europe and the United States.

CNN’s Sunaina Karkarey and Jim Bittermann contributed to the report.

French opposition lawmakers sharply criticized President Nicolas Sarkozy’s decision to return France to NATO’s integrated military command after a 43-year absence, arguing that the move would weaken the country’s strategic independence and surrender a central part of its Gaullist legacy.

Sarkozy’s government defended the policy as a pragmatic adjustment to France’s existing role in the Atlantic alliance. France had remained a NATO member and had taken part in numerous alliance-led operations despite withdrawing from the integrated command structure in 1966 under President Charles de Gaulle. Government officials said that staying outside NATO’s military decision-making bodies limited France’s ability to shape policies in missions to which it was already contributing troops and resources.

To demonstrate that the plan had solid political backing, the government brought the issue before the National Assembly and linked it to a vote of confidence. Lawmakers approved the policy by 329 votes to 238, giving Sarkozy the parliamentary endorsement he sought. The result reflected the governing party’s majority, although the debate exposed strong divisions over France’s international role.

Socialist and other opposition politicians said the return represented an unnecessary concession to the United States and risked making French foreign policy less independent. Some critics also warned that full participation in NATO’s command structure could draw France more deeply into military operations decided by the alliance. Even some politicians sympathetic to de Gaulle’s vision expressed unease about abandoning a policy that had long symbolized France’s determination to act independently of both Washington and Moscow.

The government rejected those concerns. It emphasized that France would retain control over its armed forces and nuclear deterrent and would not automatically be required to participate in every NATO operation. Sarkozy argued that national independence did not require France to remain absent from institutions where important military decisions were being made.

Supporters of the move also noted that France had already moved steadily closer to NATO since the end of the Cold War. French forces had served alongside allied troops in the Balkans, Afghanistan and other operations, while French officers had increasingly participated in NATO structures. Formal reintegration, they said, would bring political arrangements into line with military reality and allow French commanders to hold more influential positions within the alliance.

The vote marked a major reversal of the policy adopted by de Gaulle, who removed France from NATO’s integrated military command while keeping the country in the alliance. His decision was intended to preserve freedom of action and ensure that French forces would not be placed under foreign command without national approval. NATO subsequently moved its military headquarters from France to Belgium.

Sarkozy presented reintegration not as an abandonment of French sovereignty, but as a way to increase the country’s influence in Europe and within NATO. By taking a full seat in alliance planning and command bodies, France could help shape strategy rather than merely respond to decisions made by others, his government argued.

With the National Assembly’s 329–238 vote, France took a decisive step toward deeper integration into NATO. The decision closed a chapter opened by de Gaulle more than four decades earlier and signaled Sarkozy’s intention to place France at the center of Western military cooperation while continuing to claim an independent voice in international affairs.

**French parliament backs Sarkozy’s return to NATO command**

**PARIS, France —** France’s National Assembly voted 329-238 Tuesday to support President Nicolas Sarkozy’s plan to return the country to NATO’s integrated military command, reversing a policy established more than four decades ago by Charles de Gaulle.

The vote followed a heated debate in which Sarkozy’s government tied the NATO decision to a confidence motion. Prime Minister François Fillon argued that full participation would give France greater influence over alliance strategy without compromising its sovereignty or independent nuclear deterrent.

France has remained a NATO member and has participated in alliance operations, including in Afghanistan and the Balkans. But it has stayed outside NATO’s integrated command structure since 1966, when de Gaulle withdrew French forces from the U.S.-dominated system and ordered foreign NATO headquarters and troops to leave French territory.

De Gaulle said the move was necessary to preserve France’s freedom to make its own military decisions during the Cold War. NATO subsequently moved its political headquarters from Paris to Brussels.

Sarkozy has argued that the original rationale for remaining outside the command structure disappeared with the end of the Cold War. His government says rejoining will place French officers in senior NATO posts and strengthen France’s ability to shape alliance policy while also advancing European defense cooperation.

Opposition Socialists and some traditional Gaullists accused Sarkozy of surrendering a symbol of French independence without securing sufficient concessions from Washington or NATO. Critics also warned that the decision could make it harder for France to present itself as an autonomous diplomatic power and could weaken efforts to build a distinct European defense policy.

Supporters rejected those claims, noting that France already contributes heavily to NATO missions and insisting that remaining outside the command system limits its influence rather than protecting its independence.

The parliamentary vote cleared the domestic political path for France’s formal reintegration, expected to be confirmed at NATO’s summit in Strasbourg and Kehl. France will retain control over its nuclear forces and will not automatically be required to participate in every NATO operation.

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain the political debate in France over rejoining NATO’s military command, using quotations from Laurent Fabius, Nicolas Dupont-Aignan, and Louis Giscard d’Estaing.
counterfactuals.output:
The controversy arose from President Nicolas Sarkozy’s 2009 decision to restore France’s full participation in NATO’s integrated military command. France had remained a NATO member after Charles de Gaulle withdrew it from the command structure in 1966, so the dispute was less about NATO membership than about French strategic autonomy.

Opponents portrayed reintegration as an unnecessary concession to Washington. Socialist former prime minister Laurent Fabius called it **“une faute stratégique”**—“a strategic mistake”—and argued that France was surrendering a distinctive diplomatic position without receiving a meaningful European defence capability in return. For Fabius, France could cooperate operationally with NATO while retaining the independence that allowed it to speak differently from the United States.

The Gaullist sovereignist Nicolas Dupont-Aignan framed the issue even more starkly, describing the decision as **“une rupture fondamentale dans notre politique étrangère”**—“a fundamental break in our foreign policy.” He believed it abandoned de Gaulle’s principle that France should decide for itself when and where its forces were used, and risked reducing the country to an ordinary member of an American-led Western bloc.

Supporters replied that this language exaggerated the change. UMP deputy Louis Giscard d’Estaing emphasized: **“Il ne s’agit pas d’un retour dans l’OTAN, puisque nous ne l’avons jamais quittée”**—“This is not a return to NATO, since we never left it.” France had long participated in NATO missions and structures; full reintegration, he argued, would merely give French officers greater influence over decisions that already affected French forces. Supporters also maintained that it would strengthen France’s credibility with allies and make it easier, not harder, to promote a European defence policy.

Thus, the debate opposed two conceptions of influence: critics associated influence with visible independence from the United States, while supporters believed France could exercise more influence by taking senior positions inside NATO’s command structure.
